learn.hook: Before a single brick of a metro line is laid, engineers have planned routes, budgets and timelines for years. Planning is thinking before doing.
points: Planning is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go.
Planning focuses on achieving objectives and is the primary function of management: it lays the base for all other functions.
Planning is pervasive (needed at all levels and in all departments, with different scope) and continuous (a plan is made for a period, then a new plan follows).

Planning is futuristic (it looks ahead and forecasts the future), involves decision making (choosing among alternatives) and is a mental exercise (it needs foresight, imagination and sound judgement).

example.q: Top management at Vega Motors plans a 5-year expansion, while a supervisor plans the next day's shift schedule. Which feature of planning is shown?
steps: Planning happens at the top and at the supervisory level.
Only the scope of planning differs between levels.
Planning is needed at all levels: it is pervasive.

learn.reallife: The India Meteorological Department's monsoon forecast is a planning premise for farmers, fertiliser firms and tractor makers alike: planning is futuristic.

games.title: Match the feature of planning
pairs: Lays the base for all other functions
Required at all levels and in all departments
One plan is followed by another
Looks ahead and forecasts the future

games.title: Planning true or false
items: Planning is needed only at the top level of management.
It is pervasive; every level plans, with different scope.
Plans are made for a period and then new plans follow.
Planning bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to be.
Planning is needed only if there is just one way to do a job.
It requires thinking, foresight and judgement.

quiz.q: Planning is best defined as:
options: Deciding in advance what to do and how to do it
Checking whether work is done as planned
quiz.explain: That is the standard definition of planning.

quiz.q: Why is planning called the primary function of management?
options: Because it lays down the base for all other functions
Because only top managers do it
quiz.explain: Organising, staffing, directing and controlling are done within the plans.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary means only at the top

quiz.q: Planning that involves forecasting future conditions shows that it is:
quiz.explain: Planning looks ahead into the future.

quiz.q: If there were only one possible way to do a task, there would be no need for planning. This is because planning:
quiz.explain: Planning means choosing from alternatives; with one option there is nothing to decide.
quiz.mistake: Picks 'mental exercise' because thinking is involved

quiz.q: A one-year plan of Pallavi Crafts ends in March, and a new plan begins in April based on the old one's results. This shows planning is:
quiz.explain: Plans follow one after another without a break.

quiz.q: Planning requires foresight, imagination and sound judgement. This shows planning is:
quiz.explain: It is an intellectual activity of thinking before doing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks thinking ability relates to pervasiveness

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Planning is pervasive. Reason (R): Planning is required at all levels of management and in all departments of the organisation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: R gives the meaning of pervasiveness, so it explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks planning is only for top management

quiz.q: Which feature of planning says that it is purposeful and has no meaning unless it contributes to predetermined goals?
quiz.explain: Plans are made to achieve objectives.

teach.ask: Gappu yawns: 'Why plan? I just fly wherever the wind takes me!'
teach.praise: Ha! Deciding in advance what and how, looking into the future. Maybe I'll plan my route next time!
teach.nudge: Wind isn't a plan! What does planning decide, and when does it decide it?

learn.hook: A cricket team that has planned its bowling changes doesn't panic when the opponent smashes 20 in an over. Plans calm the chaos.
points: Provides direction: it tells employees in advance what to do and how.
Reduces the risks of uncertainty: managers anticipate changes and plan for them (though risk cannot be eliminated).
Reduces overlapping and wasteful activities: plans coordinate the activities of departments and people.
Promotes innovative ideas: planning is the first function and lets managers think of new ideas.
Facilitates decision making: managers choose the best among alternatives. Establishes standards for controlling: plans give the standards against which actual performance is measured.

example.q: Without a plan, both the sales and marketing teams of Leela Foods ran separate festive campaigns for the same product. Which importance of planning was missing?
steps: Two departments did the same work twice.
Planning would have assigned clear tasks to each.
Planning reduces overlapping and wasteful activities.

learn.reallife: Before the monsoon, municipal bodies plan drain cleaning and emergency teams. Planning reduces the risk from uncertain weather, though it can't stop the rain.

games.title: Match importance to example
pairs: Every employee knows the target and route
Keeping extra stock before the monsoon
Two teams no longer repeat the same task
Brainstorming a new product during planning
Targets used to judge actual results

games.title: True or false?
items: It reduces the risks of uncertainty but cannot remove them.
Without planning, there can be no controlling.
Plans provide the standards controlling needs.
Managers think of new ideas while planning.
It reduces overlapping by coordinating activities.

quiz.q: Planning provides the standards against which actual performance is measured. This shows planning:
quiz.explain: Controlling compares actual results with standards set in plans.

quiz.q: Which statement about planning and uncertainty is correct?
options: Planning reduces the risks of uncertainty but cannot eliminate them
Planning has no link with uncertainty
quiz.explain: Managers anticipate changes, but the future can never be fully predicted.

quiz.q: A clear plan tells employees in advance what is to be done and how. This is:
quiz.explain: Knowing in advance what to do gives direction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks this is about decision making

quiz.q: Planning helps managers choose the best course from several alternatives. This importance is:
quiz.explain: Planning involves evaluating and selecting among alternatives.

quiz.q: While planning a new snack line, Kesar Foods' managers came up with a millet-based idea. Which importance does this reflect?
quiz.explain: Planning encourages managers to think of new ideas.
quiz.mistake: Thinks new ideas come only from R&D

quiz.q: Planning coordinates activities of different departments so that work is not duplicated. This is:
quiz.explain: Planning removes duplication and waste.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Planning establishes standards for controlling. Reason (R): Planning provides the goals against which actual performance is compared.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Plans set goals; controlling measures performance against them. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks planning and controlling are unrelated

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Planning eliminates the risk of uncertainty. Reason (R): Planning helps managers anticipate future changes and prepare for them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false because planning only reduces risk. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What good is a plan if the future can change anyway?'
teach.praise: So plans give direction, cut risks and waste, spark ideas and set standards. Even if the future changes!
teach.nudge: The future may change, but what does a plan still give us? Think about direction and risk.

learn.hook: Some firms make a perfect 5-year plan, then a pandemic arrives in year one. Plans have limits too.
points: Leads to rigidity: managers may feel they must stick to the plan even when circumstances change.
May not work in a dynamic environment: the environment keeps changing, and plans cannot foresee every change.
Reduces creativity: if middle and lower managers only follow plans made by top management, they get little chance to use initiative.
Involves huge costs: time and money are spent on research, experts and discussions, which may not always justify the benefits.
Is a time-consuming process: there may be little time left for action. Does not guarantee success: a good plan must still be implemented well; success also depends on execution.

example.q: Rohan Retail spent 6 months and ₹10 lakh on a market study before opening a store, by which time a rival had already opened in the same area. Which limitations are shown?
steps: The study took 6 months, leaving no time to act first.
It also cost a large sum.
This shows planning is time-consuming and involves huge costs.

learn.reallife: Several firms with rigid annual plans struggled when lockdowns hit in 2020, while those with flexible plans pivoted faster. Planning can lead to rigidity.

games.title: Match limitation to the case
pairs: Sticking to the plan despite changed conditions
May not work in a dynamic environment
A sudden new law upsets the plan
Lakhs spent on experts and surveys
A good plan fails due to poor execution

quiz.q: Managers continue with a plan even when circumstances have changed. Which limitation is this?
quiz.explain: Feeling bound to the original plan causes rigidity.

quiz.q: Middle managers at Orbit Ltd are not allowed to deviate from plans framed by the top. Which limitation is highlighted?
options: May not work in a dynamic environment
quiz.explain: Following plans without freedom limits initiative and creativity.
quiz.mistake: Picks rigidity, which concerns sticking to an outdated plan

quiz.q: A company's sales plan failed because a new competitor entered with low prices. This shows planning:
options: May not work in a dynamic environment
quiz.explain: Unexpected changes in the environment can make plans fail.

quiz.q: 'Planning creates a false sense of security.' This relates to which limitation?
quiz.explain: Managers may rely on a past successful plan, but success needs proper implementation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks false security relates to cost

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of planning?
quiz.explain: The others are importance points; time consumption is a limitation.

quiz.q: Planning needs research, experts and many meetings. Which limitation follows?
options: May not work in a dynamic environment
quiz.explain: Time and money spent on planning can be large.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Planning may not work in a dynamic environment. Reason (R): The business environment is constantly changing and every change cannot be accurately foreseen.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because changes cannot all be predicted, plans may fail. R explains A.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A well-made plan guarantees the success of a business. Reason (R): Success depends on proper implementation of the plan as well.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: plans need good execution. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If planning is so great, why do some plans fail?'
teach.praise: So plans can be rigid, costly, slow and still fail if the world changes or execution is poor. Plans aren't magic!
teach.nudge: Think of what happens when the world changes after the plan is made, or when plans cost too much.

learn.hook: A family planning a wedding sets a budget, assumes the guest count, lists venue options, compares them, picks one, books it and keeps checking. That is the planning process!
points: Step 1 Setting objectives: decide what the organisation wants to achieve; objectives flow down to departments.
Step 2 Developing premises: assumptions about the future, e.g. forecasts of demand, interest rates, government policy. All managers should use the same premises.
Step 3 Identifying alternative courses of action. Step 4 Evaluating alternative courses: weigh positive and negative aspects of each in light of objectives.
Step 5 Selecting an alternative: choose the best (most feasible, profitable, with fewest negative consequences), sometimes a combination.
Step 6 Implementing the plan: putting it into action. Step 7 Follow-up action: monitoring whether the plan is being implemented as intended.

example.q: Uday Agro assumes the monsoon will be normal and fertiliser demand will rise 10% next year. Which step of planning is this?
steps: These are assumptions about future conditions.
Assumptions that underlie plans are called premises.

learn.reallife: Before launching a new train service, railways estimate passenger demand (premises), compare route options (alternatives), choose one, start operations and keep monitoring occupancy (follow-up).

games.title: Planning process steps
games.prompt: Arrange the steps of planning in order

games.title: Spot the step
pairs: Assuming that demand will grow by 8%
Listing three possible locations for a plant
Comparing the costs and benefits of each location
Checking monthly whether the plan is on track

quiz.q: What is the first step in the planning process?
quiz.explain: Planning begins by deciding what is to be achieved.

quiz.q: Assumptions about the future on which plans are based are called:
quiz.explain: Premises are the base assumptions of planning.

quiz.q: Comparing the positive and negative aspects of each option in the light of objectives is:
quiz.explain: Evaluation weighs each option before the final choice.

quiz.q: Tejas Motors decided to set up its new plant in Gujarat after comparing four states. Which step is this?
quiz.explain: The final choice is the selection step.
quiz.mistake: Thinks comparing and choosing are the same step

quiz.q: Monitoring whether the plan is being carried out properly is called:
quiz.explain: Follow-up checks that the plan is being implemented as intended.

quiz.q: Hiring staff and buying machines to put the chosen plan into action belongs to which step?
quiz.explain: Putting the plan into action is implementation, which may involve other functions such as organising and staffing.

quiz.q: How many steps are there in the planning process as given in the NCERT book?
quiz.explain: Setting objectives, developing premises, identifying alternatives, evaluating alternatives, selecting an alternative, implementing, follow-up.
quiz.mistake: Combines identifying and evaluating into one step

quiz.q: Assertion (A): All managers in an organisation should be familiar with and use the same premises. Reason (R): Premises are the base on which plans are drawn, so using different assumptions would lead to inconsistent plans.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since premises underlie plans, different premises would make departmental plans clash. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each manager can have different premises

teach.ask: Gappu wants to plan his first migration: 'Where do I even start?'
teach.praise: Objectives first, then assumptions, then compare and choose, act and keep checking. My migration is planned!
teach.nudge: Don't fly off yet! What comes first, and what do you assume about the journey?

topics.title: Types of plans: single-use, standing, objectives, strategy, policy

learn.hook: A company's 'no credit beyond 30 days' policy is used for years, but its Diwali sale plan is used just once. Plans come in different shapes.
points: Single-use plans are made for a one-time event or project that is unlikely to be repeated, e.g. budgets, programmes and projects. Standing plans are used repeatedly for recurring situations, e.g. policies, procedures, methods and rules.

Objectives are the end results which management wants to achieve. They should be expressed in specific terms, be measurable, have a time limit and be stated in quantitative terms where possible, e.g. 'raise sales by 10% in a year'.

Strategy is a comprehensive plan for accomplishing an organisation's objectives. It covers: determining long-term objectives, adopting a particular course of action and allocating resources. It takes the business environment into account.
Policies are general statements that guide thinking or channel energies towards a particular direction, e.g. a recruitment policy or a pricing policy. They leave room for managerial discretion.

example.q: Classify: (i) 'We aim to achieve a 20% market share by 2028.' (ii) 'We will enter rural markets with low-priced sachets, backed by a ₹50 crore budget.' (iii) 'We recruit only graduates for sales posts.'
steps: (i) A specific, measurable end result = objective
(ii) A comprehensive course of action with resource allocation = strategy
(iii) A general statement that guides decisions = policy

learn.reallife: When an Indian phone maker decides to fight a global rival with low prices, online-only sales and heavy local marketing, it is framing a strategy.

games.title: Single-use or standing plan?
items: Budget for the annual sports day
Programme for launching a new product
Project to build a new warehouse
Rule against smoking in the factory

quiz.q: Which of these is a standing plan?
quiz.explain: Policies are used repeatedly; budgets, programmes and projects are single-use.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a budget is used again and again

quiz.q: A plan for organising a one-time product launch event is a:
quiz.explain: It is developed for a one-time event.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every plan is a standing plan

quiz.q: 'To increase sales by 15% in the next financial year' is an example of a(n):
quiz.explain: It states a measurable end result with a time limit.

quiz.q: A comprehensive plan that considers the business environment and decides long-term goals, course of action and allocation of resources is a:
quiz.explain: These three dimensions define a strategy.

quiz.q: 'It is our company's practice to buy raw materials only from local suppliers wherever possible.' This is a:
quiz.explain: A general statement guiding decisions with some discretion ('wherever possible') is a policy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any 'company practice' is a rule

quiz.q: Which statement about policies is correct?
options: They are rigid and allow no discretion
They are expressed only in numbers
They are general guidelines that leave room for discretion
quiz.explain: Policies guide thinking; rules allow no discretion; procedures list steps; budgets use numbers.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a dimension of strategy?
options: Listing the steps for issuing a gate pass
Adopting a particular course of action
quiz.explain: Step-by-step lists are procedures, not strategy.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Budgets are single-use plans. Reason (R): A budget is prepared for a specific period and a new one is made for the next period.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because each budget applies to one period and is replaced, it is single-use. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a budget is reused year after year

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Is a plan just one thing? My teacher said there are many types!'
teach.praise: Single-use for one-time events, standing for repeated ones, and objectives, strategy, policy each do a different job!
teach.nudge: Think of how often a plan is used. Then name some types like objective or policy.

topics.title: Procedures, methods, rules, programmes and budgets

learn.hook: 'No mobile phones on the shop floor' leaves no choice. 'Steps to claim travel expenses' leaves no doubt. Different plans, different jobs!
points: Procedure: routine steps on how to carry out an activity, in chronological order. It is meant for internal use, e.g. the procedure for granting leave.

Method: the prescribed way or manner in which a task has to be performed, given the objective, e.g. on-the-job or off-the-job training methods. Procedure is a series of steps for an activity; method is the way of doing one step or task.

Rule: a specific statement telling what is to be done or not done. No flexibility or discretion; violation may lead to a penalty, e.g. 'No smoking in the factory'. A policy is a general guide with discretion; a rule is rigid.
Programme: a detailed statement about a project, outlining objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and timing. It combines several plans for a one-time project.
Budget: a statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms, e.g. a sales budget for the year. It is a planning device and also a control device.

example.q: Classify: (i) 'Wearing a helmet in the plant is compulsory.' (ii) 'Fill form, get it signed by the HOD, submit to accounts.' (iii) 'Sales next year: ₹40 crore.'
steps: (i) A specific must-do with no discretion = rule

learn.reallife: The Union Budget is a giant numerical plan of expected income and spending: a budget in the planning sense.

games.title: Match the plan to the example
pairs: Steps for admission: form, test, interview, fee
Detailed plan to launch a new product line
Expected sales of ₹5 crore next year

games.title: Spot the difference
items: A rule allows managers to use discretion.
Rules are rigid; policies allow discretion.
A procedure lists steps in chronological order.
A budget is expressed in numerical terms.
It states expected results in numbers.
A method and a procedure mean exactly the same.
A procedure is a sequence of steps; a method is the way a task is done.
A programme may include policies, procedures and budgets.
It is a combination of plans for a project.
Violation of a rule may lead to a penalty.

quiz.q: A plan that tells the exact sequence of steps to perform an activity is a:
quiz.explain: Procedures list chronological steps.

quiz.q: 'Employees must not use the company printer for personal work.' This is a:
quiz.explain: It is a specific must-not with no discretion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a policy because it guides behaviour

quiz.q: Which plan is expressed in numerical terms and can also be used as a control device?
quiz.explain: Budgets state expected results in numbers and serve as standards.

quiz.q: Navya Bank trains new tellers through simulated counters and role plays. The chosen way of training is a:
quiz.explain: A prescribed way of performing a task is a method.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a training technique is a procedure

quiz.q: A detailed statement for launching a new hospital wing, covering objectives, staff, equipment, timeline and funds, is a:
quiz.explain: A programme sets out all the plans for a project.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a policy and a rule?
options: A rule allows discretion while a policy allows none
A policy allows discretion while a rule allows none
A policy is always expressed in numbers
quiz.explain: Policies are general guides; rules are rigid.

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Budget: no flexibility, penalty on violation
Procedure: chronological steps for an activity
quiz.explain: Only the procedure pair is correct; the others swap features of budgets, rules and policies.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the definitions of plan types

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Rules are the simplest type of plans. Reason (R): Rules do not allow any scope for discretion or flexibility.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Rules are simple because they just say what must or must not be done, with no discretion. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rules are the most complex plans

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'A rule, a procedure, a policy... aren't they all just instructions?'
teach.praise: So a rule is a strict must, a procedure is a step list, a policy guides with freedom, and a budget is in numbers. Neat!
teach.nudge: Try one difference: which one allows no choice at all, and which one lists steps?
